In Her Latest Book R. Coleman Curtis ambitiously applies concepts from social psychology, cognitive science, affective science, and behaviorism, to derive a theoretical rationale for an integrated psychoanalytic treatment model, one that incorporates behavioral, cognitive behavioral, and gestalt therapies. As if this were not enough of a task, this amalgam is

279

wed to key psychoanalytic concepts, all in an effort to build integrative models of three specific dimensions of an individual—what Curtis refers to as desire, self, and mind.

Why attempt this rich mix? Curtis argues that without such a blend our understanding of the factors contributing to therapeutic change is impoverished. Furthermore, she believes that her resulting clinical model allows each discipline to use something of what the others contribute to therapeutic action.

Curtis illuminates scientific concepts that for many clinicians may be unfamiliar territory. In chapter nine, for example, she comprehensively contrasts the brain mechanisms of top-down processing, a sophisticated, verbally based means of managing information, with bottom-up processing, a primitive, sensory-based means of understanding, with origins in survival mechanisms. Curtis's cogent descriptions of these and other concepts alone make the book a valuable read.

It is in the later half of the book that Curtis focuses on the clinical implications of integrating psychoanalysis with findings from “scientific psychology.” She spells out a definition of psychoanalytic work broad enough to incorporate a panoply of strategies for treating patients. She writes, “I maintain that a theory is psychoanalytic to the extent that it examines the possibilities of unconscious factors affecting current experiences, is thoughtful about the way such factors may be affecting the patient-therapist relationship, considers the potential usefulness of analyzing the patient-therapist relationship in the therapy, and considers conflict” (p. 13).

Where Curtis may surprise psychoanalysts of most persuasions is in her contention that transference analysis is overly emphasized in psychoanalytic therapy.

In Memoriam—Bertram H. Schaffner, M.D.

1912-2010

THE EDITORS AND STAFF of Contemporary Psychoanalysis mourn the loss of Dr. Bertram Schaffner, pioneering psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, author, and researcher. We cherish Dr. Schaffner as a brave and wise colleague. His compassion, skills, and deep understanding of human nature inspired generations of psychoanalysts and other mental health professionals. Dr. Schaffner was a gay man in the forefront of clinicians who practice openly as gay professionals, who deal openly with gay issues, and who work to enhance the dignity and self-esteem of professionals in our field.

Bertram Schaffner was born in 1912 in Erie, Pennsylvania. He entered Harvard University at the age of 15. He transferred to Swarthmore College, where he received his A.B. in 1932. He graduated from Johns Hopkins Medical School in 1937, trained in neurology at Mt. Sinai Hospital, and did his psychiatric residency at Bellevue Hospital and the New York Psychiatric Institute.

Dr. Schaffner served in the military during World War II and played a role in the Nuremberg trials after the war. He undertook psychoanalytic training at the William Alanson White Institute from 1949 to 1953- He was in private practice steadily since 1947. He was a faculty member and clinical supervisor at the White Institute since 1960 and served as President of the William Alanson White Society in 1960. He was the Medical Director of the HIV Clinical Service from 1993 to 2000 and was also a co-leader, with Dr. Stuart Nichols, of a landmark support group for HIV-positive medical professionals. He was appointed Supervising Analyst at White in 1994.

The film Mine Own Executioner, released in England in 1947, is worth our attention because of the authenticity of its depiction of analytic psychotherapy, the dramatic and visual manner with which it explores the possibilities and limitations of the treatment itself, and the convincing portrayal of the psychotherapist's conflicts and struggles in response to the treatment. The film is also notable for its dramatic exploration of such issues as lay analysis, war neuroses, the schizoid personality, and schizophrenia. Finally, the film offers us the opportunity to explore the relationship between narrativity in film and psychotherapy with some help from Freud's concept of Nachträglichkeit.

SOME PLACE QUITE UNKNOWN is Jane Lazarre's most recently published novel. She is the author of several works of fiction, as well as a comparable number of works of nonfiction, all autobiographical memoirs.

464

The sense and style of memoir, in fact, pervades this novel and there are many autobiographical components in this purportedly fictional work. What makes this book notable, and appropriate for a book review in an analytic journal, is that it is actually a novel about a psychoanalysis, or at least about psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy (Lazarre herself studied at an institute for two years). The entire novel is essentially an (attempted) journey into the unconscious, with side forays into quotidian life, as it is elicited in an analytic treatment that seems to span about three or four years in the book. The novel and the analysis are woven around a pivotal childhood traumatic event, the suicide of the protagonist's mother. The protagonist's name is Celia; she tells us that her name is a limb of that of her aunt, Lucille, just as her niece, Lia, has been given a piece of her name. This name-play seems designed to underscore the generational connections between women and their female offspring, one of the motifs of the book.

“Some place quite unknown”—a line from a letter written by Celia's mother—becomes a metaphor for the journey of analysis. The one-page prologue practically summarizes the whole book.

A woman in her fifties begins to have unbidden, compulsive suicidal fantasies. She indulges them even though she has no conscious wish to kill herself, despite certain recent disappointments, despite the defining fact of her emotional life: her mother killed herself when this woman was a child of eight. Then one day she is crossing the street and is nearly hit head on by a car. She knows she saw the car, that the near “accident” was somehow intentional [p. 11].

She is a woman with a full, rich, and gratifying life; a wife in a stable marriage of long duration; a mother of a capable, sensitive adult son; a gifted teacher and writer—and yet, “In the center she is trying to map a journey backward in time in a realm other than ordinary life, the realm of barely conscious memory, of conscious secrecy, of imagery and feelings beyond words, of dreams” (p. 11). Now, she says, she is writing the record of her “extraordinary experiences with Dr. Daniels” (p. 16).

In Prologue to Violence, Abby Stein tells of a 15-year-old boy who killed a 63-year-old woman. The young murderer described his actions in the following way: “I just started stabbing her. I really did not think about it. I really did not want to stab anybody. It was just bad luck” (reported by Revitch and Schlesinger, 1989, p. 1). Most forensic professionals

*I would like to thank Dr. Emily Kurifoff, who worked painstakingly and skillfully to help shape this review.272

would likely focus their evaluation of this case on the teen's conscious intentions, fantasies, and defective sense of right and wrong. Stein, on the other hand, traces the genesis of this and other acts of violence to dissociation, trauma, and reenactment. In making her argument she is thorough in her documentation of violent criminals' histories and accounts of their crimes. Stein provides abundant data, derived from open-ended interviews she conducted with incarcerated inmates, archival data in police files, and quantitative research. As a work of applied psychoanalysis, Stein's book is exemplary.

Stein is equally rigorous in her application of multiple theoretical perspectives to the phenomenology of violence. While she uses a broad array of psychoanalytic, attachment, forensic, and cognitive neuroscience theory to help us understand the many factors that conspire to create humans capable of terrible deeds, she mostly focuses on the power of trauma and dissociation. As she puts it, “[I]t is the pathological disengagement precipitated by early, intense, and repetitive trauma that most strongly facilitates the streaming of an unprocessed violent past into the present” (p. 4). By closely examining the words and histories of these people, Stein shows how violent individuals reenact their childhood traumas in remarkably symbolic, psychologically meaningful ways. Thus psychoanalytically hospitable clinicians will find Stein's basic conclusion highly compelling, if not altogether convincing. Even the most skeptical and cynical reader will likely find it difficult to finish the book without at least finding her thesis plausible.

The dreams of athletes demonstrate that dreaming plays a direct role in motor learning processes. But beyond that, the athletic action of a dream, carrying metaphoric and symbolic significance, is an imagistic vehicle for the portrayal of the dreamer's affective and interpersonal experiences and challenges. Representation in this motor-perceptual realm of action reflects the central role that such physicality has in the developmental genesis of core affective experiencing. In light of the athletic dimension of every child's development, particular attention to imagery of the self in motion enhances access to the emotional and motivational undercurrents of life for dedicated athletes and for many other dreamers.

In this volume, Ron Aviram has synthesized social cognitive psychology and our modern Relational psychoanalytic perspective so as to understand prejudice better. Examining an issue from more than one orientation is very close to the way I was trained in the Department of Social Relations at Harvard some 40 years ago. Aviram's scholarship once again demonstrates how such different areas of study can enrich our knowledge.

The author, beginning with a summary of the major themes of prejudice, presents the work of Freud, Adorno, Fromm, Brewer, Allport, Tajfel, and others. He makes sure that the reader can see the potential for overlap in these ideas, and his explications also set the historical context for the different viewpoints. It is also clear that Aviram is writing about the individual's experience of the large group and how important this is in understanding prejudice from a Relational perspective. For example, he criticizes Adorno's position that prejudice can be minimized by eliminating “the stereotypical ingroup-outgroup distinction and all that goes with it” (p. 148). Instead Aviram believes that one first identifies with the family, and then with the societal group, and that this is “necessary and unavoidable” (p. 16). Any individual can be placed on a continuum from overidentification to underidentification with the large group. Aviram's basic position is that “[p]rejudice occurs when there is a loss of optimal balance in the capacity to be an autonomous individual while experiencing belonging to the large group” (p. 5).

For the most part, we do our work in the dark, shrouded and held in secrecy, privacy, confidentiality. In Dare To Be Human, Israeli

599

psychoanalyst Michael Shoshani Rosenbaum dares to expose in detailed particularity what transpired between him and his extraordinary patient, Daniel, during the course of their seven-year psychoanalytic treatment. Daniel himself contributes two sections written posttermination. In its extensive exploration of the effect of analyst and patient on each other, including careful tracking of countertransference experience, sources, and expression in enactments, this intimate testimony constitutes a mighty and unique contribution to our field. Through nuanced, but largely jargon-free writing, Shoshani succeeds in speaking to two audiences: He writes to demystify the psychoanalytic process for nonprofessional readers with limited knowledge and exposure to our work. He writes also for the professional analytic community—experienced clinicians and students of psychoanalysis for whom the book could well serve as a sophisticated teaching text. For this audience of colleagues, Shoshani has provided copious scholarly footnotes throughout, referencing sources in psychoanalysis, philosophy, and literature. He also includes a final, more theoretically oriented chapter written expressly for the analytic community; here he circles back to offer a more complexly formulated analysis of such issues as the nature of therapeutic action in his work with Daniel, the use of differential therapeutic modalities (Freudian, Relational/Interpersonal, self-psychological), and questions relating to termination.

Shoshani captures, in clear, evocative, at times poetic language, the contradictory and multifaceted quality of profound, long-term psychoanalytic work, with its dialectics of control versus spontaneity and restraint versus passionate participation. In addition, he communicates a sense of the inevitable imperfection of treatment and particularly, in his words, the “non-ideal” nature of this analyst and this treatment. Although Shoshani conveys this imperfection with a sense of humility—that is to say, he is open with us about his doubts during the treatment and discusses several instances when he apologized to his patient for hurtful actions and blindspots—there is also an overly certain, at times all-knowing and even self-congratulatory quality that comes across in some of his interventions with Daniel, as well as in some of his sweeping pronouncements to us his readers. This problematic tone, which periodically creeps into the book, as well as a sometimes heavy-handed citing of the luminaries in our field, contribute to some of the ways I feel the book itself is imperfect or “nonideal.

Drescher and Merlino's American Psychiatry and Homosexuality: An Oral History offers readers a new experience. Earlier books

268

narrated the history of the depathologizing of homosexuality—sometimes as a political process (Bayer, 1981), and other times as a scientific paradigm shift (Rosario, 2002). Kenneth Lewes's (1988) masterwork, Psychoanalysis and Male Homosexuality, comprehensively integrated both perspectives. Yet this volume provides access to 17 verbatim interviews, enabling the reader to “visit” with activists—both gay and straight—who coalesced at a particular moment in social history. These men and women disturbed the medical establishment and provoked a leap in civil rights.

For instance, the book includes an interview with Robert Spitzer, who chaired the American Psychiatric Association (APA) Nomenclature Committee. He recalls the professional climate prior to 1973: “Pretty much everybody who was trained in those years took it for granted that homosexuality was not just an illness, but it was a very severe illness. It was considered not just an illness of sexual functioning, but really a widespread personality disturbance” (p. 99).

Gay psychoanalyst Bertram Schaffner describes how that belief system fostered a climate of distrust and fear. Homosexual physicians could lose their jobs, as Shaffner once did. He recounts that gay physicians could also lose their medical licenses for what was then called “moral turpitude” (p. 200).

We read the story of Stuart Nichols, Director of New York Beth Israel's Detoxification unit in the mid 1970s. Nichols recalls an evening when a distraught “macho” patient came to him in tears with a new awareness that he might be gay. Fearing his own exposure, Nichols recalls being unsympathetic, cold and nonreassuring to the patient. Nichols recalls feeling tormented two days later after learning that the patient had committed suicide.

In the book's pages we also learn of the secret community created in the midst of such danger. Prior to 1973, gay psychiatrists (self-dubbed the Gay-P-A) would network in secret locations, often at gay bars, during the annual meeting of the APA. Nanette Gartrell recalls her surprise that not one of more than 100 psychiatrists wore a name badge.

The title of Mark Blechners new book, Sex Changes, is a double entendre depending on whether one reads the word changes as a verb or a noun. That is, sex changes. It changes from culture to culture, from one point in history to another, and from one individual to another. The result of these changes is what Blechner also calls “sex changes”— the multiple variations in human sexuality and practices. I believe that the book's most significant contribution is its revelation of the various ways psychoanalysts have been, and continue to be, prejudiced against this variability, and how becoming aware of our narrow mindedness can only help us as practitioners and as human beings. Blechner's stance throughout the book is “queer” in the sense that it espouses understanding and acceptance rather than judgment, marginalization, and pathologizing. It is, in Blechner's words, “tolerance of the unusual” (p. 167).

Blechner claims that psychoanalysis was once a queer theory because of its emphasis on sexuality, polymorphous perversity, and the unconscious. I agree with him and have sadly noted a “desexualization” in psychoanalytic theory in recent decades (Knafo, 2006). André Green (1995) has astutely commented that something important is lost when we avoid speaking about sexuality and the body. Blechner's book is, then, a welcome, straightforward, and personal account of many issues that may be neglected in psychoanalytic circles and training today.

The format Blechner chose for his book is unusual and refreshing. It is a collection of papers he wrote on the subject over a period of 35 years (from 1972), with introductions to each paper written from his present perspective. Sex Changes is thus a rare blend of the personal, theoretical, clinical, and political.

In Her Clinically Rich, Comprehensive Book Making a Difference in Patients' Lives, Sandra Buechler begins her chapter on empathy by describing her interaction with two patients, Arlene and Anna. These descriptions illustrate Buechler's particular ideas about therapeutic action, or how she “makes a difference” with patients. Returning to treatment one year after termination, Arlene is sad and weary, tearfully reflecting on the reasons for her unhappiness, trying to pin down its causes objectively. First Buechler resonates with her patient's misery. Quickly, though, she finds herself recovering from this identification and begins to reflect on what is happening. She wonders about Arlene's missing joy and resolves to inquire about it. Anna, vulnerable to narcissistic injury because of a childhood of extreme isolation and depression, comes into session in an agitated state—nerves jangled, words tumbling out at a fast clip in a strained, high-pitched voice. Feeling swept up in this agitation but resisting being swept away by it, Buechler feels her way out of her reaction by being curious within herself about her own response and the patient's agitation. At the same time, she is recovering her internal emotional balance. She remains calm with the patient, sits back in her chair, and speaks slowly in a measured tone.

In Buechler's view, therapeutic change grows out of such moments of affective exchange between patient and analyst. The patient expresses and enacts her problematic affect state with the analyst, and Buechler is affected, resonating with the patient's state and possibly feeling what it is like to be the object of this state as well. Momentarily, Buechler gives herself over to her reaction, allowing her emotional equilibrium to be disrupted. Then, however, moving out of her immersion in her reaction, she enlists her own coping skills and becomes curious about what has just occurred and what the action reveals about the patient, the analyst, and their relationship. Buechler finds that she will privilege themes in her subsequent inquiry that reflect what she has discovered about this process of emotional disruption and recovery, a result of her curiosity. She suggests that the patient then benefits from her process in several ways.

Understanding the ubiquitous human phenomena associated with sports requires a “depth” psychology like psychoanalysis, among other theoretical tools. Sports exemplify basic Freudian concepts, such as unconscious motivation, unconscious conflict and compromise, and the centrality of sexual, aggressive, narcissistic, and attachment themes throughout the human life cycle. Sports also provide powerful illustrations of some of the important recent developments in psychoanalytic theory, including Lacan's work on the Imaginary and Symbolic registers; Kohut's psychology of the self and the role of selfobjects in development; Butler's feminist-psychoanalytic theories on performativity, gender binaries, and the unmourned losses at the root of gender; Laplanche's “general theory of seduction”; and the work of the psychoanalytically influenced sociologist Rene Girard. Finally, sports have a natural kinship with psychoanalysis because both involve the interrelationships among the intrapsychic, interpersonal, and social realms.

trauma, certainty, Wittgenstein, rites of passage, religious conversion

Wittgenstein's explorations into the social functions of certainty show that we live within a network of unquestioned rules. Trauma disrupts these unquestioned certainties, substitutes new, authoritative convictions, and exiles the traumatized person from his or her previously shared world. Wittgenstein helps us see how the repetitive communications so familiar in traumatic reactions are attempts to overcome this exile by seeking a resonant understanding in the listener. When the exiling truths of trauma are acknowledged by another, a community of understanding is reestablished; some prior certainties may be regathered, and healing can occur. The disruption and restitution of certainties play a central role in certain forms of religious conversion and in rites of passage. These examples illustrate the importance of certainty as an organizing aspect of human experience.

This essay examines sports as a repository for both idealized and degraded parts of self-experience. Sports as action and fantasy catalyze a variety of nostalgic longings, including wishes to resurrect positive experiences from childhood as well as to create false, idealized fantasies about who we wish we were then and now. Sports also contain degraded elements of self that result from attempted reconciliation between playful fantasy and realistic disappointment. Athletes, as the containers of these idealized fantasies, are ambivalently held objects, adored but also hated because they can never live up to the longed-for idealization. The author also examines our longing for a time when play was our job and the suspension of disbelief in sports was a shorter jump from everyday life than the responsibilities and stresses of adult life allow. Nostalgia and the recollection of our sports heroes and our own achievements allow us to dip back into that treasure chest of memory and, of course, fantasy.

CHRISTOPHER LUKAS'S SECOND, MORE PERSONAL BOOK on the aftermath of a suicide1 is a gem in its historical detail and contextual richness, yet frustrating because of the contradiction between the assertions he makes and the narrative he presents. That is, while Lukas claims that “blue” genes or genes that correlate with depression and bipolar illness are inherited, the story that he tells suggests otherwise. Understandably, Lukas is trying to make sense of the multiple suicides2 that have devastated his family, including the more recent suicide of his brother, two-time Pulitzer Prize winning author J. Anthony Lukas, which rattled him enough to set this book into motion. While Lukas wonders whether his brother's death was preordained, at the same time, and perhaps unwittingly, he provides substantial evidence that suggests a more complex interplay between biochemistry and unmourned traumatic loss.

To my mind, the story of the author's brother's suicide begins much earlier in time, with the tragic and troubled relationship between Lukas's mother, Elizabeth, and his grandmother, Missy.

Although Elizabeth would like to free herself from her mother's intrusive control, she is beset by terrible anxiety when she does act more autonomously. These dynamics emerge most dramatically when Elizabeth makes her first suicide attempt; they can also be seen in the most immediate events that lead up to her actually taking her life.

psychoanalysis, psychotherapy, envy, malignant, intersubjectivity, development

Comparing various psychoanalytic perspectives on envy and malignant envy, the author argues for a developmental reconsideration of envy that locates its emergence in the breakdown of intersubjectivity. This breakdown is connected with the inability of the mother/analyst to hold and contain the child's/patient's affective states such that the child/patient is deprived of being recognized as a subject. Moreover, the dyad is unable to experience fully the pleasure and enjoyment of a reciprocal, mutual, and intimate relationship. This developmental failure interferes with the patient's capacity to experience and act on her desire. Unable to to sustain a link with the other's mind, the child cannot take in and then hold on to good, pleasurable experiences. The author illustrates his argument with two clinical examples, those of a child patient and of an adult patient. The child case highlights the breakdown of intersubjectivity as a developmental precursor to envy, whereas the adult vignette emphasizes the relationship between destructive envy and the perversion of desire.

Object Relations in Contemporary Psychoanalysis

Contrasting Views

Harold Blum MD

Harold Blum

Harold Blum   Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, New York University School of Medicine; Executive Director, Sigmund Freud Archives; and former Editor, Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association.
object relations, countertransference, unconscious conflict, fantasy, co-construction;

Object relations perspectives have contributed greatly to the contemporary concept of a two-person analytic process, even among traditional psychoanalysts. With the recognition of intersubjectivity, the caricatured ideal of the affectless, neutral analyst has been replaced by a model of an empathie analyst with therapeutic interest and sufficient neutrality and objectivity. Object relations theories have also been important in the changed understanding of countertransference from a focal blind spot to a ubiquitous influence that can advance analytic progress. “Minding the gap” between the different schools, I describe and briefly comment on the contrasting views of relatively traditional or mainstream theory and practice, and object relations theory and practice. I discuss the shift from a one-person focus on the intrapsychic conflicts of the patient to both a one and a two-person analytic process. I consider countertransference as well as transference; the emphasis on “here-and-now” analytic relationships; analytic change effected through interpretation and insight versus change through the dyadic object relationship and experience; and the analyst as new and real object alongside the analyst as a transference object. From a theoretical perspective I address object relationships as the necessary precursor and foundation for psychic structure formation within the tripartite structural theory and as contrasted with and contributed to by object relations theory. Object relations versus instinctual drive theory and the notions of external object relationships versus unconscious self- and object representation and internalized object relations are also discussed.

psychotherapy, psychoanalysis, dissociation, gender, trauma, development

The discovery that free association can undo dissociation is the psychological equivalent to discovering fire. Psychoanalysis began with this discovery, but its liberatory promise became constrained. With the shift in emphasis from dissociated knowledge to the unconscious, a cure through love became wedded to miracle, mystery, and authority. In the 1970s, as winds of liberation swept through society, the authority of psychoanalysis was questioned and its patriarchal underpinnings exposed. Free association, it turned out, had been bound to the voice and law of the father. The question raised by Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor becomes a question for our time: was he right in his assessment that people find love and freedom too burdensome? Research in developmental psychology and neurobiology suggests he was not and points to the ways that tensions within psychoanalysis mirror tensions between democracy and patriarchy and reflect the dissonance between a voice grounded in the body and emotion and a voice wedded to what we now recognize as a false story about ourselves.

For many American psychoanalysts the couch is the default position used with all analytic patients. This paper reviews empirical studies of the relation between the patient's position, sitting or lying, and free association. Findings are inconsistent; the patient's position may have an effect in some dyads and not in others. There have been no studies of a possible relationship between the patient's position and therapeutic outcome. Therefore, there is no empirical foundation for putting all analytic patients on the couch. We propose that selection of a position for the patient requires a careful, empathic, flexible, clinical judgment by the analyst, including consideration of the analyst's own theory, as well as of the patient's personality characteristics and diagnosis.

This essay proposes that the formative years of psychoanalytic theory and praxis were affected by the fascism, war, and genocide in their midst. That this impact was largely absent from analytic discourse throughout most of the 20th century may be attributed to a number of factors. Analysts at the time had hopes for a positivist psychoanalysis—a “new science”—both universal and independent of context. Subjective experiences of the trials and expulsion of mostly Jewish professionals were thus viewed as a threat to the status of both the theory and its practitioners. Some analysts may have also been reluctant to dwell on their ordeal because they felt lucky to be alive and to start anew, unlike those left behind. Finally, the relative silence on the topic may represent a response to trauma, to experiences so overwhelmingly conflictual as to be only partially appreciated, or at times adaptively dissociated. Focusing as much on what has been omitted as on what is included in writings and interviews of analysts from the period, this discussion attempts to discern a presence in absence, noting the style and tenor of the work that theorists and clinicians left behind, all in an effort to find traces of a personal and collective catastrophe that altered theoretical and clinical ideas.

This article describes three attitudes toward psychic pain and suffering, and their clinical implications are explored and illustrated. When analyst and patient differ fundamentally in their understanding of the place of suffering in psychic life, treatment destructive clashes may result. The attitude that pain should be reduced as quickly as possible has a significant impact on the analyst's focus in treatment, most especially on the timing of interpretations of defense. A third possibility embraces suffering as not only unavoidable, but as a primary source of wisdom and personal identity.

Relational psychoanalysis represents the composite of contributions from a variety of psychoanalysts, all of whom found dissatisfaction in their clinical work with patients where the restrictions of the classical psychoanalytic approach led to unsatisfactory or less than optimal outcomes with their patients. While some have emphasized the technical limitations of classical psychoanalysis, others have rejected the classical theory of causality and the central role of insight and interpretation. Whether on the basis of technical or theoretical differences, relational psychoanalysts have placed greater emphasis on the role of the relationship between analyst and patient in accounting for the therapeutic action of psychoanalysis. What has evolved is distinctly different from, indeed, oppositional to, classical psychoanalysis. Therefore, the attempt to homogenize relational and classical approaches risks the possibility of obscuring the significant differences between them. If such a homogenization occurs, psychoanalysis loses the status of a clinical discipline that must stay open to changes in practice that reflect the experience of those who employ it in their clinical work.

In on Deaths and Endings: Psychoanalysts' Reflections on Finality, Transformations, and New Beginnings, editors Willock, Bohm. and Curtis offer clinicians an embarrassment of riches. Many of the book's chapters tackle themes that are vastly undertheorized and underreported in the analytic literature. The 24 papers, gleaned from a symposium on the subject, range from intensely moving accounts of direct clinical work with dying patients to theoretical discussions of shifting understandings of the death instinct, metaphoric deadness of significant members of patients' families, and analyses of poetry, myth and film. Reviewing such a collection invariably involves considerable “deciding.” Such “deciding,” Foster Wallace (2008) points out, “reflects the reviewer's bias as much as the inherent value of any of the chapters in the book” (p. xiv). There's no way to give adequate or equal attention to all the chapters, and the choice that I am making is to focus on those which are about actual death, not metaphoric death. For, as Anna Aragno states at the start of her excellent essay,

It is, however, the personal encounter with death and its severance of a cherished relationship that hurtles us into an adaptive crisis from which we cannot emerge but transformed. The irrevocability of death makes this a loss like no other. Though we summon prior coping mechanisms nothing adequately prepares for this final separation. The intensity of pain and degree of psychosocial upheaval is such that we fear we will not survive. Yet we do … by laboring through a painful, lengthy process in a disorganized state gradually modulating affect, habituating to change and memorializing a relationship [p. 21].

*I dedicate this review to Mary Dunn, who died on September 4, 2008, and to my former student and colleague, Helene Nemiroff, who remained a therapist to the end, which came on July 18, 2002.

One key source of our current conceptual diversity is a shift to an epistemology based on the radical idea that we can learn most about experience by studying experience itself rather than by looking for the causes of it. The resulting emphasis on experience-near, clinically based conceptualizations has left us awash in a pluralism of diverse, irreconcilable perspectives. The press in the field is toward ever-closer descriptions of our clinical work, to rethink anew our process without the encrustations of theory. In our attempts to describe process, we act on a necessary illusion. On one hand, our attempt to grasp the living moment of our clinical experience in tradition is an effort to preserve a vital activity for posterity. On the other hand, it risks calcifying creativity and belief into dogma. The resolution to this risk is a critical “humorous” acceptance of multiple perspectives from the open ground of an epistemológica! pluralism. The hope in our field is that it is grounded in a process that ever transcends our attempts to grasp it even as we discover, create and preserve the living act that we do.

I offer the view that the source of therapeutic action in psychoanalysis is a shared minding of the dissociative gap—a process that simultaneously decreases the mind's fear of otherness and the vulnerability of the brain's neural networks to potential affect dysregulation. Through a patient's “me” and “not-me” self-states becoming more at home with each other, the automatic neurosynaptic warning signal that triggers immediate dissociation as a protection against potential hyper-arousal becomes more selective at the brain level and, through a feedback loop, allows the patient's mind to support increased development of intersubjectivity. Little by little, the patient's capacity to bear internal conflict is increased by easing the mental struggle to hold it cognitively. For a classical psychoanalyst, taking this seriously does not lead to abandoning Freud, but it does lead to a different listening stance. It requires listening to clinical process not only dyadically, but listening to it as an inherently confusing affective event to be processed together, rather than as content to be “understood”; that is, organized by the analyst into something he deems cognitively conceptual and then made available for potential interpretation. Clinical examples are provided for consideration.

ACCORDING TO WRITING ABOUT PATIENTS, there are many reasons why psychoanalysts include case material in their publications. They hope to achieve prestige in the field, to understand how psychoanalysis works, or to reflect on and digest a powerful experience with a patient.

469

Psychoanalytic writing has always depended on the use of clinical information to enliven theoretical papers, and the single case study is a time-honored tradition in our field dating back to Freud.

Until fairly recently, clinical material used in professional writing was considered to be “owned” by the psychoanalyst. Disguising a patient's identity from friends and family was the unofficial professional standard for publication. Two factors have dramatically changed this position. The first is the evolution of psychoanalytic theory from a one-person to a two-person model. That is, psychoanalytic process and content are increasingly viewed as cocreated by analyst and patient. It is therefore less likely that the analyst will make unilateral decisions regarding writing for the public. Second, the Internet has transformed accessibility to all published material. Twenty years ago it would have been unlikely that patients not in the field would come across their analysts' writings. Now one can simply “Google” one's therapist and potentially recognize oneself in the text of any publication. For these and other reasons, Kantrowitz's topic is timely and useful.

Despite acknowledging the challenges inherent in using case material, Kantrowitz takes the position that “[i]t is necessary for clinicians to expose their work and their thinking about it—for themselves as well as for other clinicians and for psychoanalysts” (p. 306). Even after an exhaustive exploration of difficulties weathered by analysts and patients alike, the author concludes by reminding us that clinical writing introduces new ideas into the field. She claims that published material provides wider dissemination of current thinking than supervision or local seminars can, and that case examples make theory come alive. Analysts need to report what they do in order to learn from each other, Kantrowitz continues, and also to inform the psychoanalytic community about current practices. Finally, she reminds us that writing about patients can help analysts to overcome blind spots and can stimulate intellectual curiosity and growth. Clearly, the question for Kantrowitz is not if, but when and how actual case material should be included in our literature.

This Lively volume is intended to educate Western psychoanalysts who are largely unfamiliar with the history and influence of psychoanalysis in India. Divided into three sections—Mind, Body, and Spirit—the

chapters analyze myth, literature, spirituality, movies, and politics using psychoanalytic theory to make comparisons and connections between Indian and Western psychologies.

We learn of its surprisingly early beginnings in 1921 when Girindrashekhar Bose published The Concept of Repression. Indian scholars have thus been aware of and alive to European ideas about character and the unconscious for quite some time. They have also developed uniquely Indian approaches to psychoanalytic thinking in order to accommodate important cultural differences, such as child development within the complex extended family and the “pervasiveness of religious or spiritual practice” (p. 16). Akhtar and Tummala-Nara acknowledge that these distinctive contributions can also be undercut by “colonial terminology, [which] continues to prevail in the psychoanalytic writings on Indians, by both Indian and non-Indian analysts” (p. 19). The authors give an egregious example in the work of Kurtz, who attributes the ease of Indian children's attachment to nonfamilial female figures to a lack of bonding and implicit rejection by the biological mother. The authors quote Kurtz as saying that “healthy, empathie mirroring seems to be entirely absent here” (p. 15). He describes the impact of multiple mothering as “breaking] the heart of the self, and resulting in narcissistic withdrawal, if not schizoid regression.” Akhtar and his coauthor call this conclusion “racist and incredible” (p. 15). They offer numerous counterarguments and attribute Kurtz's conclusions to Western anthropologists' focus on poverty-ridden households.

Ironically, however, this discussion is followed by a rather narrow-minded chapter by Prakash N. Desai and Hyman L. Muslin regarding Gandhi's “self.” Pathologizing Ghandhi's political and spiritual values, these authors attribute them to a profound fear of his own and other peoples' aggression. Desai and Muslin also claim that because of this fear Gandhi was unable to transcend his mentors, to boldly risk new involvements that offered a more varied means by which to make political and social changes. In this way the authors diminish Ghandhi's contribution to the future of India and the world. Their approach contrasts sharply with that of other psychoanalytic biographers (particularly Erik Erikson, 1969), who have linked Gandhi's subjective experience to his rich spiritual life, rather than limiting his motives to psychological problems that fit too neatly into Freudian drive theory.

The author addresses the question of the misrepresentation of psychoanalysis and psychoanalysts in the media and suggests that Freud's theory of man's psyche has, at its center, the inevitable and subversive contradiction that all knowledge undermines the narcissistic certainty of the knower; specifically, the unconscious mind constantly works to unseat that which is available to consciousness. This truism, which is the theoretical and clinically demonstrable position of psychoanalysis, produces resistance and aversion to the discipline, its practice, and its practitioners. The author argues, with brief references to three works of art, that paradoxically, by virtue of this misrepresentation of psychoanalysis—of its ideas and praxis, its very worth, and its contribution to society and to culture—the discipline of psychoanalysis is convincingly upheld.

The portrayal of psychoanalysts in films and on television is usually a far cry from being a realistic depiction. As professional consultant to a TV series, I initially believed that my task was to uphold the public reputation of analysts; but, as I became further involved, I realized that the shortcomings and failures of analysts are essential to good drama. Films do not attempt to represent the actual reality accurately but rather to convey an inner reality. The analyst as protagonist becomes a far more interesting character once we observe him dealing with his conflicts, weaknesses, and limitations. Filmmakers attempt to allow for our authenticity and humanity and permit the analyst to enact well beyond what may be considered acceptable, not because they want to denigrate him but rather to show the fragile human being behind the professional. My role as consultant was to try to assure accuracy in the depiction of the analyst's work and at the same time to allow the drama to reach those dangerous and dark places that our work does not ordinarily traverse but that nevertheless represent our deepest wishes and anxieties.
